name: I-V-vi-IV (Axis progression)
aka: i-bVI-bIII-bVII (the same loop heard from the relative minor)
why: Three major chords frame one minor chord, so the loop sounds hopeful with a single shadow, and every rotation can serve as the start.

name: 50s progression
examples: Stand by Me - Ben E. King
why: The tonic drops to its relative minor and climbs back through IV and V, the gentle rocking loop of 1950s ballads.

name: I-IV-vi-V
examples: She Drives Me Crazy - Fine Young Cannibals
why: The 50s loop with vi and IV swapped, so the minor chord arrives late and V pulls straight back home.

name: I-vi-iv-V (Sleep Walk changes)
why: The 50s loop with its IV turned minor, which adds a dreamy, bittersweet sigh before the dominant.

name: I-IV-V (three-chord song)
examples: Twist and Shout - The Isley Brothers
why: Tonic, subdominant and dominant in their plainest order, the three-chord engine of rock and roll, folk and country.

name: I-bIII-IV-bIII (Sonics' Louie Louie)
why: Swapping the V of the Louie Louie loop for a borrowed bIII gives the garage-rock riff a darker, bluesier edge.

name: I-bVII-IV (double plagal)
examples: Sweet Child o' Mine - Guns N' Roses
why: Each chord falls a fourth to the next, two plagal steps in a row, so the loop feels open and anthemic rather than resolved.

name: I-bVII-IV-V (Mixolydian)
why: A Mixolydian descent through bVII and IV that turns back up to V, mixing rock swagger with a real cadence.

name: I-V-bVII-IV (chromatic descending 5-6 sequence)
why: Two pairs of chords a fifth apart, the second pair a whole step below the first, so the loop slides down with a relaxed, open sound.

name: i-bVII-bVI-bVII (Aeolian shuttle)
examples: All Along the Watchtower - Bob Dylan / Jimi Hendrix
Somebody That I Used to Know (chorus) - Gotye
why: The minor tonic steps down two whole steps and back up, a brooding rock loop with no leading tone.

name: i-bVII-bVI (Aeolian descent)
examples: Con el bate de aluminio - Los Van Van
Stairway to Heaven (final section) - Led Zeppelin
why: Three chords walk straight down the natural minor scale, a heavy, fatalistic fall that loops back up to the tonic.

name: I-III-IV-iv (Creep progression)
why: A major III brightens the loop and then IV turns minor, so hope and disappointment trade places every bar.

name: Major line cliche (I-I+-vi-I+)
why: One inner voice creeps up from the fifth to the sixth and back over a held tonic bass, giving a single chord a sense of motion.

name: bVI-bIII-bVII-IV-I (extended plagal)
aka: Circle of fourths into the tonic
examples: Hey Joe - The Jimi Hendrix Experience
why: Five major chords a fourth apart chain plagal steps all the way home, a long rolling fall into the tonic.

name: Hotel California progression
aka: Spanish progression (as described for this song)
why: Each pair of chords falls a fourth, so the minor loop drifts through bright major chords before the dominant pulls it back.

name: bVII-V7-I cadence
examples: (Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay - Otis Redding
why: A borrowed bVII leans onto the dominant seventh before home, the twangy cadence of 1960s rock and Western scores.

name: bIII-V7-I cadence
why: A borrowed bIII sets up the dominant with a surprising, slightly dark lift before it resolves.

name: IV-iv-I (plagal sigh)
examples: Wake Me Up When September Ends - Green Day
why: The IV darkens to iv, its sixth sinking a half step onto the fifth of the tonic, a sentimental sigh before home.

name: I-I7-IV-iv
aka: Plagal turnaround with a dominant-seventh tonic
examples: The Japanese Grand March (earliest cited source)
why: The tonic grows a seventh that pulls it to IV, and IV then turns minor, a churchy, bittersweet way back to the start.

name: I-iii-IV (Puff schema)
examples: Puff, the Magic Dragon - Peter, Paul and Mary
Let's Get It On - Marvin Gaye
why: The mediant triad slips in between tonic and subdominant, a soft, folky step that delays the lift to IV.

name: i-bIII-iv (minor Puff)
examples: The House of the Rising Sun - The Animals
why: The minor tonic rises to its relative major and on to iv, a ballad shape that sounds warm and fatalistic at once.

name: i-bVII-bVI-v (Aeolian lament)
examples: I Don't Like You - Eva Simons
why: The Andalusian descent ending on a minor v, so the cadence stays modal and never sharpens to a leading tone.

name: i-bVII-bVI-iv
why: The lament descent skips the dominant and lands on iv, so the loop sinks without any pull back to the tonic.

name: i-bIII-IV-bVI
why: The roots climb through the minor pentatonic scale, with a bright major IV that hints at Dorian.

name: bVI-V-i-bIII (minor Hopscotch)
why: The Hopscotch loop heard in minor with a true dominant, so the climb into the tonic gets a sharp leading-tone pull.

name: I-iii/7-IV/6-V7 (major descending bass)
examples: I'll Follow the Sun - The Beatles (variant)
why: The bass walks down 1-7-6-5 under gentle inversions, a major-key cousin of the lament that lands on a half cadence.

name: Descending chromatic bass in major
why: The bass slides down chromatically under the tonic while IV turns minor, a wistful major-key cousin of the lament.

name: Minor chromatic line descent
why: The bass creeps down by half steps under a held minor tonic, turning one chord into a slow, haunted descent.

name: i-i/b7-IV7/6-bVI (While My Guitar Gently Weeps)
examples: While My Guitar Gently Weeps - The Beatles
why: The bass steps down from the minor tonic through a Dorian IV7 to the flat sixth, a weary, sliding lament.

name: i-i/b7-viø7-bVImaj7 (Dream On)
why: A half-diminished chord on the raised sixth sits in the middle of the falling bass, borrowing melodic-minor colour on the way down.

name: ii-V-I
why: The supertonic and dominant sevenths fall by fifths into a major-seventh tonic, the basic cadence of jazz.

name: Minor ii-V-i
aka: 7-3-6 (gospel name, heard from the relative major)
why: A half-diminished ii and an altered dominant fall into a minor tonic, darker and more urgent than the major cadence.

name: ii-bII7-I (tritone substitution)
examples: April in Paris (minor form, mm. 11-12) - Vernon Duke
why: The dominant is swapped for the dominant a tritone away, so the bass slides down by half steps into the tonic.

name: Backdoor progression (IV-iv7-bVII7-I)
why: The tonic is approached from the flat side through borrowed minor chords, a softer, more wistful arrival than V-I.

name: I-vi-ii-V turnaround
examples: Island in the Sun - Weezer (as vi-ii-V-I)
why: A two-bar circle of fifths that leaves the tonic and arrives back on the dominant, the standard way to keep a tune turning over.

name: I-VI7-ii7-V7 turnaround
why: Turning vi into a dominant seventh gives the turnaround a secondary-dominant pull into ii, a brighter, more urgent swing.

name: iii-vi-ii-V
why: The circle of fifths started from the mediant, so the turnaround avoids the tonic until the very end.

name: Ragtime progression (VI7-II7-V7-I)
examples: Sweet Georgia Brown - Ben Bernie & Maceo Pinkard
why: A chain of dominant sevenths, each resolving down a fifth to the next, bounces back to the tonic.

name: II7-V7-I
why: The supertonic becomes a dominant seventh, so it pushes into V like a second leading chord before home.

name: #iv°7-V-I
why: A diminished seventh on the raised fourth leans onto the dominant by half step, a ragtime and parlour cadence.

name: ii-bIII+-I
why: An augmented chord on bIII shares the dominant's leading tone and adds a raised fifth, a smoky substitute for V.

name: Back-cycled ii-V chain
aka: ii-V substitution of the ragtime progression
why: Each dominant of the ragtime chain gets its own ii, so pairs of chords fall by fifths in a long spiral home.

name: iii7-bIII7-ii7-bII7-Imaj7
why: Tritone substitutes put every other chord a half step lower, so the bass walks chromatically down to the tonic.

name: Rhythm changes A section
why: Fast two-beat turnarounds circle the tonic, then a I7-IV-iv move borrows the plagal sigh before the cadence.

name: Rhythm changes bridge (Sears Roebuck bridge)
examples: Scrapple from the Apple (bridge) - Charlie Parker
why: Two bars of each dominant seventh walk the circle of fifths back toward the home key.

name: Montgomery-Ward bridge
examples: On the Sunny Side of the Street - Jimmy McHugh
why: Two ii-V pairs climb a whole step from IV to V, the jazz descendant of the galant Monte sequence.

name: Stomp progression
examples: King Porter Stomp - Jelly Roll Morton
Bojangles (A Portrait of Bill Robinson) - Duke Ellington
why: A IV7, raised-fourth diminished and tonic six-four shuffle ends in a ragtime turnaround, the swing-era riff chorus.

name: Coltrane changes (Countdown substitution)
why: Keys a major third apart are each touched by their own dominant, so one cadence spins through three tonal centres.

name: Tune Up changes (ii-V-I down a whole step)
why: The same ii-V-I is played and then moved down a whole step, so the key centre sinks like a staircase.

name: Tadd Dameron turnaround
why: Chords borrowed from the flat side fall by fifths and then by half step, a lush chromatic way back to the tonic.

name: I-bIII7-II7-bII7 turnaround
why: Tritone substitutes for vi and V make the bass slide down by half steps from bIII to the tonic.

name: I-biii°7-ii7-V7 turnaround
why: A diminished seventh slides down by half step into ii, a gospel-tinged passing chord inside the turnaround.

name: Autumn Leaves A section
aka: Circle of fifths in minor (jazz form)
why: A ii-V-I in the relative major is answered by a ii-V-i in the minor, two cadences linked by the circle of fifths.

name: All the Things You Are A section
examples: All the Things You Are - Jerome Kern
why: Roots fall by fourths from vi to IV, then one dominant lifts the tune a major third into a new key.

name: Lady Bird changes
why: Backdoor ii-Vs visit the flat keys and a closing Dameron turnaround slides home, a sixteen-bar loop full of soft chromatic colour.

name: Solar changes
why: A minor-major tonic opens a chain of ii-V-I cadences that keeps stepping down to new keys until a minor ii-V brings it back.

name: So What / Impressions form
aka: Modal AABA, Dorian a half step apart
why: Sixteen bars on one Dorian minor seventh, eight a half step higher and eight back, so the colour comes from the mode rather than from chord changes.

name: Maiden Voyage changes
why: Suspended dominant chords move in four-bar blocks, so the harmony floats without ever cadencing.

name: Take the A Train A section
why: Two bars of II7 with a raised fourth in the melody give the tonic a bright, whole-tone lift before a ii-V brings it home.

name: Minor line cliche
why: One voice slides down by half steps from the root inside a held minor chord, the classic sound of a brooding intro.

name: Twelve-bar blues
aka: Shuffle form with bar 12 on I
why: Four bars of tonic, two of subdominant and a dominant-subdominant turnaround, the call-and-response frame of the blues.

name: Twelve-bar blues, quick change
why: Bar 2 jumps to IV and back, so the form moves sooner and swings harder than the slow change.

name: Bebop (jazz) blues
why: The twelve-bar form with ii-V approaches, a raised-fourth diminished and secondary dominants, so every bar points to the next.

name: Bird blues (Bird changes)
why: Descending ii-V pairs replace the plain blues chords, spiralling down by whole and half steps before the turnaround.

name: Minor blues
why: The blues form in a minor key, with a bVI7 falling by half step onto the dominant for a darker turnaround.

name: Eight-bar blues (Key to the Highway)
examples: Key to the Highway - Big Bill Broonzy
why: The dominant arrives in bar 2, so the short form swings between I, V and IV in quick, conversational phrases.

name: Eight-bar blues (Worried Life Blues)
why: Two bars each of tonic and subdominant, then a quick I-IV, I-V turnaround, probably the most common eight-bar blues.

name: Eight-bar blues (Heartbreak Hotel)
why: Four bars of brooding tonic before a short IV-V-I close, a stark eight-bar blues with all its weight up front.

name: Eight-bar blues (Walkin' by Myself)
why: Four bars on the tonic and then one bar each of IV, V, I and V, an unorthodox eight-bar shape that rushes the ending.

name: Eight-bar blues (Trouble in Mind)
why: A minor iv and a secondary dominant give this gospel-tinged eight-bar blues a sweeter, more song-like turn.

name: Eight-bar blues (Sitting on Top of the World)
examples: Sitting on Top of the World - Howlin' Wolf
why: The tonic seventh leads to IV and a borrowed iv before a dominant and a double turnaround, a country-blues eight-bar.

name: Eight-bar blues (Ain't Nobody's Business)
why: A major III, a borrowed iv and a vi-ii-V turnaround give the eight bars a torch-song shape.

name: Eight-bar blues (twelve-bar minus its first four)
examples: Mary Had a Little Lamb - Buddy Guy
Love Me Like a Man - Bonnie Raitt
why: Starting on the subdominant drops the listener straight into the second line of a twelve-bar blues.

name: Sixteen-bar blues (extended tonic)
why: Eight bars of stop-time tonic before the usual twelve-bar ending, so the tension builds on one chord.

name: Sixteen-bar blues (repeated middle)
examples: Going Down the Road Feeling Bad - Woody Guthrie
why: The IV-to-I line is sung twice before the turnaround, a folk-blues form that stretches the middle.

name: Sixteen-bar blues (repeated turnaround)
why: The V-IV turnaround is played three times in a row, so the end of the form hangs in a groove before landing.

name: I-IV vamp (plagal)
examples: Oh Happy Day - Edwin Hawkins Singers
In the Midnight Hour - Wilson Pickett
why: Tonic and subdominant rock back and forth, the open, churchy groove behind gospel vamps and soul verses.

name: IV-V-bVI-bVII-I (4-5-b6-b7-1)
why: Two diatonic steps and two borrowed ones climb by step into the tonic, a dramatic gospel ending.

name: i-iv-V7 (minor three-chord)
why: Minor tonic and subdominant with a major dominant, the harmonic-minor engine of slow jams and street-guitar songs alike.

name: I-vi two-chord vamp
why: Tonic and relative minor share two notes, so the vamp rocks gently between bright and soft.

name: Pachelbel's Canon progression
examples: Don't Look Back in Anger - Oasis
why: The bass falls a fourth and rises a step in a repeating pattern, so the chords descend gracefully while staying bright.

name: Romanesca (galant schema)
why: A stepwise-falling bass under alternating root-position and first-inversion chords, the noble opening gambit of the galant style.

name: Prinner
aka: Modulating Prinner (the same schema in the dominant key, I-V/7-#iv°/6-V)
why: The bass steps down 4-3-2-1 under a falling upper line, the galant style's gentle answer to an opening phrase.

name: Fonte
why: A cadence onto minor ii is repeated a step lower in the major, so the phrase descends like water from a fountain.

name: Monte
why: Each secondary dominant resolves up a step, so the phrase climbs like a mountain path toward the dominant.

name: Ponte
why: The dominant is held like a pedal while the melody climbs, a bridge that builds expectation for the return of the tonic.

name: Do-Re-Mi (galant schema)
why: The melody rises do-re-mi over tonic, dominant and tonic again, a simple and confident opening.

name: Meyer
why: The tonic moves to the dominant and back while the bass steps 1-2-7-1, a balanced question-and-answer opening.

name: Sol-Fa-Mi
why: The melody falls 5-4-4-3 while the bass rises to ii and returns through the leading tone, a courtly opening gambit.

name: Fenaroli
why: Two dominant-tonic pairs with the bass climbing 7-1-2-3, a circular figure that keeps turning around the tonic.

name: Quiescenza
why: Over a tonic pedal the upper line sinks to the flat seventh and climbs back, a calm closing gesture after a cadence.

name: Indugio
why: The subdominant is lingered on before the bass rises to the raised fourth, a deliberate delay before the cadence.

name: Cadenza semplice
why: The bass climbs 3-4-5 into the dominant and drops to the tonic, the plain galant cadence.

name: Cadenza composta (cadential six-four)
why: A tonic six-four over the dominant bass delays the V7, the grand compound cadence of classical music.

name: Cadenza doppia
why: The dominant is held while a six-four and a suspended fourth resolve above it, an ornate, ceremonious cadence.

name: Converging cadence
why: The bass climbs chromatically 3-4-#4-5 to a half cadence while the melody falls, the voices converging on the dominant.

name: Deceptive cadence (galant)
why: The bass climbs to the dominant and then steps up to vi instead of falling to I, a cadence that sidesteps its goal.

name: Diatonic circle of fifths (major)
examples: Angels We Have Heard on High (refrain)
why: Every diatonic chord is visited by falling fifths, a sequence that feels unstoppable and returns to its start.

name: Diatonic circle of fifths (minor)
why: The minor-key circle passes through the relative major before the dominant pulls it back to the minor tonic.

name: Rule of the octave (ascending)
why: Each step of a rising major-scale bass gets its standard Baroque chord, so a plain scale becomes a full progression.

name: Rule of the octave (descending)
why: The falling scale is harmonised with a brief tonicisation of V on the sixth degree, a model for accompanying any descending bass.

name: Lament bass (diatonic)
examples: Por una Cabeza (chorus, variant) - Carlos Gardel
why: The bass descends four steps from tonic to dominant under soft minor inversions, the Baroque emblem of grief.

name: Chromatic lament bass (Dido's Lament)
examples: Dido's Lament (When I am laid in earth) - Henry Purcell
Crucifixus (Mass in B minor) - J. S. Bach
why: The bass sinks by half steps from tonic to dominant, each chromatic step adding weight to the mourning.

name: Phrygian half cadence
examples: Schau, lieber Gott, wie meine Feind (BWV 153) - J. S. Bach
why: The bass falls a half step from the flat sixth to the dominant, an archaic, questioning close in minor.

name: Ascending 5-6 sequence
examples: For Unto Us a Child Is Born (underlying harmony) - G. F. Handel
why: Each chord shares its bass with the next and then the bass steps up, so the music climbs one scale degree at a time.

name: Descending 5-6 sequence
aka: Descending thirds with passing first inversions
why: Root-position chords alternate with first inversions over a stepwise-falling bass, a smooth, singing descent.

name: Up-a-fourth, down-a-third sequence
why: Roots rise a fourth and fall a third, so each pair of chords sits a step above the last in a cheerful climb.

name: La Folia (later folia)
examples: Trio Sonata Op. 1 No. 12 - Antonio Vivaldi
Variations on a Theme of Corelli - Sergei Rachmaninoff
why: A slow sarabande ground that swings between minor tonic, dominant and the relative major, built for endless variation.

name: Romanesca (Renaissance ground)
examples: Guardame las vacas - Luys de Narvaez
why: A ground that starts in the relative major and slides into the minor and back, a staple of sixteenth-century improvisation.

name: Passamezzo antico
why: Minor tonic and subtonic alternate, then the relative major and the dominant, the Renaissance ground behind countless dances.

name: Passamezzo moderno
aka: I-IV-bVII-IV (the same loop heard from IV, Mixolydian)
examples: Honky Tonk Women - The Rolling Stones
why: Tonic alternates with subdominant and dominant in two balanced strains, the major-key Renaissance ground that folk song inherited.

name: Neapolitan cadence
examples: Moonlight Sonata (first movement) - Ludwig van Beethoven
Piano Sonata in C minor - Joseph Haydn
why: The flat second, voiced over the fourth degree, darkens the approach to the dominant with a poignant half-step fall.

name: Italian sixth cadence
examples: Piano Sonata Op. 78 (second movement) - Ludwig van Beethoven
why: The flat sixth in the bass and a raised fourth above it squeeze outward by half step onto the dominant.

name: German sixth cadence
examples: Appassionata Sonata (slow movement) - Ludwig van Beethoven
why: A chord that sounds like a dominant seventh on the flat sixth resolves through a cadential six-four, a rich approach to V.

name: Picardy third cadence
examples: Jesu, meine Freude - J. S. Bach
why: A minor progression that ends on a major tonic, so the final chord arrives like light after shadow.

name: Tristan chord resolution
examples: Prelude to Tristan und Isolde - Richard Wagner
why: A half-diminished chord melts onto a dominant seventh that never reaches its tonic, the emblem of Romantic longing.

name: Moravian cadence
why: The outer notes of an added-sixth subdominant move inward by a tone onto a first-inversion tonic, a soft folk-like close.

name: i7-IV7 (Dorian shuttle)
aka: ii7-V7 vamp (the same loop heard as a ii-V)
examples: Oye Como Va - Tito Puente / Santana
why: The major IV carries the raised sixth of the Dorian mode, so the minor vamp sounds cool and groovy rather than sad.

name: i-bIII-bVII-IV (Mad World)
why: A minor tonic answered at the end by a major IV, so the loop hovers between minor gloom and Dorian brightness.

name: i-bVI shuttle
why: The minor tonic and the major chord on the flat sixth share two notes, a stark, sorrowful two-chord rock.

name: I-bVII (subtonic shuttle)
examples: Tired of Waiting for You - The Kinks
You Really Got Me (verse) - The Kinks
why: Tonic and the major chord a whole step below alternate with no dominant, the loose, swaggering sound of Mixolydian rock.

name: I-II (Lydian shuttle)
examples: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial (main theme) - John Williams
why: The major II brings in the raised fourth, so the tonic seems to float upward with wonder.

name: II-IV-I (Lydian cadence)
why: The Lydian II falls to IV and then home, a sunny cadence that avoids the dominant entirely.

name: i-bII (Phrygian vamp)
why: The half step above the minor tonic gives a menacing, exotic pull, the core of Phrygian metal riffs.

name: i-bII-bIII (Phrygian climb)
why: The riff climbs a half step and then a whole step from the minor tonic, a dark, heaving Phrygian figure.

name: i-bVI-iv-bVII
why: The minor tonic falls to bVI and climbs back through iv and bVII, a modal loop with no leading tone.

name: bVI-bVII-i (Aeolian cadence)
aka: IV-V-vi (4-5-6 gospel rise, the same loop heard from the relative major)
examples: The Fellowship theme (The Lord of the Rings) - Howard Shore
why: Two major chords climb by whole step into a minor tonic, a heroic but sombre arrival.

name: I-bVI (chromatic mediant)
aka: I-III (the same major-third pair heard from the other chord)
examples: Symphony No. 3, second movement - Johannes Brahms
why: A major chord a major third below shares one note with the tonic, a sudden, glowing shift of colour.

name: I-bIII (chromatic mediant)
aka: I-VI (the same minor-third pair heard from the other chord)
why: A major chord a minor third above the tonic shares one note with it, a bold, cinematic lurch.

name: I-bvi (doubly chromatic mediant)
why: A minor chord a major third below the major tonic shares no notes with it, an uncanny, otherworldly shift.

name: I-biii (doubly chromatic mediant)
why: A minor chord a minor third above the major tonic has no common tones, a dark, disorienting jolt.

name: i-bvi (minor chromatic mediant)
examples: Gollum's theme (The Lord of the Rings) - Howard Shore
why: Two minor chords a major third apart share one note, a progression that film music uses for evil, power and menace.

name: I-iv (minor plagal)
why: A borrowed minor iv over a sustained tonic gives a bittersweet, longing glow.

name: I-bVI-IV
examples: An Ideal of Hope (Man of Steel) - Hans Zimmer
why: A borrowed bVI between tonic and IV casts a shadow over a heroic major key, heroism with a threat underneath.

name: bVImaj7-v-i-v7
why: A major-seventh bVI and a minor v soften the minor key, so the loop feels vast and less lonely.

name: bVI-bVII-I (Mario cadence)
aka: Aeolian cadence with a Picardy third
examples: Super Mario Bros. level-end fanfare - Koji Kondo
why: Two chords borrowed from the minor climb by whole steps into a major tonic, a triumphant fanfare ending.

name: Andalusian cadence
examples: Hit the Road Jack - Ray Charles
why: Four chords step down the minor tetrachord to a major chord on the fifth, which flamenco hears as a Phrygian home.

name: i-bvii-bVI-V7 (Andalusian with minor bvii)
why: Making the second chord minor smooths the descent and gives the cadence a darker, more modal colour.

name: Solea por arriba (letra accompaniment)
why: Over two twelve-count compases the tonic rises through its seventh to iv and falls back down the Phrygian tetrachord, the solemn heart of flamenco.

name: Flamenco cambio (bII-bVI-bII-I)
why: Moving from bII to bVI briefly sounds like the relative major before the half step back down to the Phrygian tonic.

name: Farruca compas (V7-i)
why: Dominant seventh and minor tonic alternate in four-count bars, a stern, proud minor pulse.

name: Farruca llamada (iv-i-V7-i)
why: The subdominant leads into a plain minor cadence, the A-minor close that ends farruca phrases.

name: Fandango de Huelva copla
why: The sung copla leaves the Phrygian tonic for the relative-major area and falls back through bII, the classic fandango shape.

name: Guajira (flamenco) letra
why: A Cuban-flavoured major song form in flamenco's twelve-count compas, swinging between tonic and dominant with a vi-ii turn.

name: Girl from Ipanema A section
examples: The Girl from Ipanema - Antonio Carlos Jobim
why: A Lydian-tinged II7 floats over the tonic before a ii and a tritone-substitute dominant glide down by half step home.

name: Blue Bossa changes
why: Minor ii-V-i cadences frame a brief ii-V-I a half step up, a cool, sunlit minor bossa.

name: I-IV-V-IV
examples: Louie Louie - Richard Berry / The Kingsmen
El Loco Cha Cha - Rene Touzet
why: The V falls back to IV instead of resolving, so the loop circles endlessly, ideal for a dance groove or a montuno.

name: i-bVII (double tonic)
examples: Somebody That I Used to Know (verse) - Gotye
why: The tune swings between a minor tonic and the chord a whole step below, the modal heartbeat of English, Scottish and Irish song.

name: Double tonic with dominant close
why: The double-tonic shuttle is closed with a real dominant, a tune shape that leads straight into the passamezzo antico.

name: I-V7 two-chord vamp
examples: Achy Breaky Heart - Billy Ray Cyrus
why: Just home and the dominant seventh, the simplest harmonic swing of folk dances, polkas, country and the alegrias compas.

name: Freygish vamp (I-bvii)
why: The major tonic of freygish alternates with a minor chord a whole step below, whose third gives a half-step pull back to the tonic.

name: Hijaz vamp (I-bII)
why: The flat second over a major tonic outlines the Hijaz augmented second, a hypnotic, exotic sway.

name: Royal road progression (IVmaj7-V7-iii7-vi)
aka: bVImaj7-bVII7-v7-i (the same loop heard from the relative minor)
why: Subdominant and dominant climb, then the expected tonic is replaced by iii and vi, a bittersweet lift that J-pop choruses love.

name: Royal road with ii-V-I
why: The royal road keeps falling by fifths after vi until it reaches the tonic, turning the loop into a full cadence.

name: IVmaj7-V7-III7-VI7 (royal road with secondary dominants)
